dataset_family: INTERCEPTOR project (Italian AIFA/Ministry of Health multicentre MCI cohort, 351 MCI followed for 3 years); healthy controls recruited outside INTERCEPTOR
method_family: Resting-state 19-channel scalp EEG: relative spectral power, delta/alpha ratio, magnitude-squared coherence and small-world index (electrophysiology)
what_it_shows: Pappalettera et al. (2025), Alzheimer's Dement TRCI 11:e70194. Of 351 INTERCEPTOR MCI patients, 116 were positive for both hippocampal atrophy and an AD-pattern FDG-PET, the combination with the highest conversion risk (48.28%). They were split into 56 who converted to dementia and 60 who stayed stable (sMCI-resilient) over 36 months, and compared with 50 external HC. Baseline EEG: converters had widespread higher relative delta power than stable patients (FDR), lower frontal alpha 1 and alpha 2 power, and a higher delta/alpha ratio. Stable patients had stronger anterior alpha coherence and a higher alpha-2 small-world index. Hippocampal volume (AdaBoost and FreeSurfer, left and right) was lower in converters on all four measures, but no difference survived Bonferroni correction (uncorrected p 0.15, 0.09, 0.06, 0.02).
why: Identity: the PDF's title, authors (Pappalettera ... Rossini) and DOI 10.1002/trc2.70194 match the block and the map. I read the whole extract to the references. STATED = partly. Part shown: a functional measure (resting EEG) distinguished future converters from stable MCI in a stratum where hippocampal volume did not discriminate after correction. Not shown: volume is not 'preserved'. Every participant was selected FOR hippocampal atrophy (and abnormal FDG-PET), so the regime is 'atrophic but non-discriminative', and atrophy already present at the MCI baseline does not support 'late'. There is no prediction model or AUC. NARROWED = yes, scoped to this selected stratum. Within MCI already positive for hippocampal atrophy and AD-pattern FDG-PET, baseline EEG separated 36-month converters from stable patients (FDR-corrected electrode tests), while continuous hippocampal volume did not (Bonferroni). The four volume p-values also fail Benjamini-Hochberg, so the null is not only an artefact of strict correction. This is information beyond volume status, comparable to P-478's finding within its high-volume subgroup. Caveats that weaken it: (1) Range restriction by design. Volume was used to select the sample, and all four volume measures trend lower in converters (uncorrected p = 0.02 for FreeSurfer right). The study therefore does not show that volume carries no information, and no joint model tests EEG beyond continuous volume. (2) The contrasts are group-level and electrode-wise only. (3) Converters had lower MMSE (24.5 vs 26.04) and more family history of dementia; the authors report that most EEG features were robust to these covariates, with the details in the supplement. (4) Conversion to dementia was a clinical diagnosis, and the HC were recruited outside the cohort. Independence: INTERCEPTOR is not a current supporter's dataset. P-1124 reports the same INTERCEPTOR cohort; it is not a supporter or a candidate, but the two must never both be counted. No authors are shared with supporters or other candidates. Method family: scalp EEG spectral and connectivity measures. Whether EEG and MEG (P-584 and candidate P-488) count as one electrophysiology family is an operator decision; both are resting-state spectral electrophysiology. Not a preprint. In the quotes, line-break hyphens are normalised; the em dashes and plus-minus signs are kept.

quotes.quote: Within the Italian INTERCEPTOR project, we investigated electroencephalography (EEG) markers of resilience in MCI individuals who exhibited reduced hippocampal volume and abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) at baseline but remained stable and did not progress to dementia after 36 months.
The highest observed conversion risk was found in the combination of hippocampal volume and AD FDG-PET pattern (48.28%).

This subgroup included a total of 116 individuals, 60 of whom remained clinically stable or reverted to normality (one subject) and did not progress to dementia. These individuals will hereafter be referred to as sMCI-resilient. The remaining 56 participants, who converted to dementia during follow-up, will be referred to as cMCI.
No significant differences after Bonferroni correction were observed between groups, confirming their comparable biological profiles.

Group comparisons were performed using independent-samples t-tests for continuous variables and chi-square for categorical variables and corrected with Bonferroni method. No results emerged after correction.
whereas cMCI converters exhibited a widespread—and statistically significant—increase in slow-wave activity compared to resilient (FDR threshold = 0.045).
sMCI-resilient individuals maintained significantly lower delta/alpha ratios in frontal regions than HC, as well as a low ratio across the scalp compared to cMCI.

Results suggested that, although some trends are observable, the majority of EEG features were robust enough to the potential confounding effects such as age, sex, education, family history, and baseline cognitive performance.
